title: Trigonometry for Any Triangle: Sine Rule, Cosine Rule and Area
description: The sine rule and cosine rule for non-right-angled triangles, the area formula half ab sin C, and two-step problems including 3D diagonals (IGCSE Maths 0580 Extended).

notes.heading: Naming Sides and Angles in Any Triangle
notes.body:
📌 Definition
In triangle $ABC$ the angles are capital $A$, $B$, $C$ and each side takes the LOWERCASE letter of the angle it faces: side $a$ is opposite angle $A$, side $b$ opposite $B$, side $c$ opposite $C$.

🔑 How it works
Draw the triangle, write the letters at the corners, then label each side by the angle straight across from it. Every rule in this topic is a statement about matched (side, opposite-angle) PAIRS.

💡 Worked Example
If you know angle $A$ and side $a$, you already hold one complete pair — exactly what the sine rule needs.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Labelling a side by the angle it touches instead of the angle it faces. Side $a$ must NOT touch angle $A$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The angles of any triangle sum to $180^\circ$ — use this to find the third angle the moment two are known.
• The largest side is opposite the largest angle, and the smallest side opposite the smallest angle: a free sanity check on answers.

✅ Check
In a triangle with angles $35^\circ$, $65^\circ$ and $80^\circ$, the longest side is the one opposite $80^\circ$.

notes.heading: The Sine Rule for a Missing Side
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The sine rule links each side to the sine of its opposite angle:

$$\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$$

It works for ANY triangle, not just right-angled ones.

🔑 How it works
Use it when you have a complete PAIR (a side and its opposite angle) plus one more angle:
1. Match the unknown side with its opposite angle.
2. Rearrange into $\text{unknown} = \dfrac{\text{known side} \times \sin(\text{its angle})}{\sin(\text{paired angle})}$.

💡 Worked Example
Angles $A = 35^\circ$ and $B = 65^\circ$ with side $a = 10$ cm. Then

$$b = \dfrac{10 \times \sin 65^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ} = 15.8 \; \text{cm}$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Multiplying by the wrong sine. The side you KNOW goes on top of the fraction, multiplied by the sine of the angle you WANT.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• You always need one side-and-its-opposite-angle pair to start.
• Bigger angles face bigger sides — if your answer reverses the order, the sines were swapped.

✅ Check
With $a = 6$, $A = 30^\circ$, $B = 90^\circ$: $b = 6 \sin 90^\circ \div \sin 30^\circ = 6 \div 0.5 = 12$.

notes.heading: The Sine Rule for a Missing Angle
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Solve the sine rule for an angle by TURNING THE FRACTIONS UPSIDE DOWN:

$$\dfrac{\sin A}{a} = \dfrac{\sin B}{b} = \dfrac{\sin C}{c}$$

Then $\sin A = \dfrac{a \times \sin B}{b}$ and $A = \sin^{-1}(\text{that value})$, in degree mode.

🔑 How it works
You need a complete pair plus one more side. The angle you want is the one OPPOSITE that extra side.

💡 Worked Example
$a = 9$, $A = 40^\circ$, $b = 7$. Then $\sin B = \dfrac{7 \times \sin 40^\circ}{9} = 0.500$, so $B = 30.0^\circ$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying $\sin^{-1}$ to a ratio built from the WRONG sides — the sides must be the one you want the angle for, and the one from your complete pair.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $\sin^{-1}$ on a calculator always returns an ACUTE angle here, which is what IGCSE asks for; if the triangle clearly has an obtuse angle instead, subtract the calculator answer from $180^\circ$.
• A safer existence check: the wanted angle must be smaller than $180^\circ$ minus the angles already known.

✅ Check
In the worked example $b = 7$ is shorter than $a = 9$, so $B = 30.0^\circ$ being smaller than $A = 40^\circ$ is exactly right.

notes.heading: The Cosine Rule for a Missing Side
notes.body:
📌 Definition
When you know TWO SIDES and the angle BETWEEN them, the cosine rule finds the third side:

$$a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A$$

The angle $A$ must be the INCLUDED angle — sitting between the two known sides.

🔑 How it works
1. Check the angle you have is between the two sides you have.
2. Substitute carefully, keeping every sign.
3. Take the square root at the end (the formula gives $a^2$, not $a$).

💡 Worked Example
$b = 5$, $c = 8$, $A = 60^\circ$: $a^2 = 25 + 64 - 2 \times 5 \times 8 \times \cos 60^\circ = 89 - 40 = 49$, so $a = 7$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Obtuse angle
$b = 6$, $c = 10$, $A = 120^\circ$: here $\cos 120^\circ = -0.5$, so $-2 \times 6 \times 10 \times (-0.5)$ becomes $+60$ and

$$a^2 = 36 + 100 + 60 = 196, \qquad a = 14$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that cos of an OBTUSE angle is negative: the minus sign in the formula then turns into a plus, so the side opposite an obtuse angle always beats both others.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• When $A = 90^\circ$ the term $2bc \cos A$ vanishes and the rule becomes Pythagoras — a good memory hook.
• Square-root at the end: leaving $a^2 = 49$ as the answer drops the final mark.

✅ Check
An obtuse angle of $120^\circ$ must sit opposite the longest side: 14 is indeed longer than 6 and 10.

notes.heading: The Cosine Rule for a Missing Angle
notes.body:
📌 Definition
With ALL THREE SIDES known, rearrange the cosine rule to find an angle:

$$\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$$

Here $a$ — the side you want the angle OPPOSITE — stands alone on top with the minus sign.

🔑 How it works
1. Put the wanted angle's opposite side into $a$ (the one being subtracted).
2. Work out the fraction, then press $\cos^{-1}$ in degree mode.

💡 Worked Example
$a = 7$, $b = 5$, $c = 3$: $\cos A = \dfrac{25 + 9 - 49}{2 \times 5 \times 3} = \dfrac{-15}{30} = -0.5$, so

$$A = \cos^{-1}(-0.5) = 120^\circ$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
A NEGATIVE value for $\cos A$ means an OBTUSE angle between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ — $\cos^{-1}$ on a correct calculator returns it directly, so do not 'fix' the minus away.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Only the cosine rule (not the sine rule) can find an angle from three sides.
• The largest angle of a triangle is opposite the longest side — start there if the question asks for the biggest angle.

✅ Check
If the three sides give $\cos A = -0.5$, the angle is $120^\circ$, and every other angle in that triangle must be acute.

notes.heading: Area of Any Triangle: Half ab sin C
notes.body:
📌 Definition
For any triangle, given two sides and the angle BETWEEN them:

$$\text{area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times a \times b \times \sin C$$

where $C$ is the included angle between sides $a$ and $b$. The letters can be renamed freely — what matters is two sides and their included angle.

🔑 How it works
Compare with 'half base times height': $b \sin C$ is precisely the perpendicular height, which is why the formula works for slanted triangles.

💡 Worked Example
Sides $7$ cm and $9$ cm with included angle $50^\circ$: area $= 0.5 \times 7 \times 9 \times \sin 50^\circ = 24.1$ cm².

💡 Worked Example 2 — Equilateral triangle
All angles are $60^\circ$, so side $8$: area $= 0.5 \times 8 \times 8 \times \sin 60^\circ = 27.7$ cm².

⚠️ Common Mistake
Plugging a NON-included angle. If the angle is not between the two sides, find or compute the one that is first.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Keep the $0.5$ — a missing factor of $2$ is the most common error mark lost here.
• Units are square (cm²), because area multiplies two lengths.

✅ Check
Sides $6$ and $10$ with included angle $120^\circ$: area $= 0.5 \times 6 \times 10 \times \sin 120^\circ \approx 26.0$ cm².

notes.heading: Which Rule, and Two-Step Problems
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Match the data you have to the tool:
• pair (side + opposite angle) plus another angle or side → **sine rule**;
• two sides and the included angle, wanting the third side → **cosine rule**;
• three sides, wanting any angle → **cosine rule**;
• two sides and included angle, wanting area → **half ab sin C**;
• nothing above? Find the third angle with the $180^\circ$ sum first — it often creates the pair you need.

💡 Worked Example — two steps
Angles $A = 35^\circ$, $B = 65^\circ$, side $a = 10$ cm: the third angle is $C = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 65^\circ = 80^\circ$, then the sine rule gives $c = \dfrac{10 \times \sin 80^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ} = 17.2$ cm.

💡 Worked Example 2 — 3D
To find the angle a cuboid's diagonal makes with its base: first get the base diagonal (a right-angled triangle in the floor), then take a vertical cross-section and use $\tan$ = height / base-diagonal. Every 3D trig question is two flat right-angled triangles wearing a trench coat.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Blindly trying the cosine rule without an included angle, or the sine rule with no completed pair — the data decides, not habit.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Round only at the END; keep full calculator accuracy between steps.
• Sanity-check with the order: biggest angle ↔ biggest side.

✅ Check
Given sides $9$ and $12$ with included angle $40^\circ$, first find the third side with the cosine rule — then decide which rule unlocks the angles.

flashcards.definition: In triangle ABC, side a is opposite angle A, side b opposite B, side c opposite C.
flashcards.example: Side a never touches corner A.

flashcards.definition: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
Flip it: sin A/a = sin B/b = sin C/c, then use the inverse sine.

flashcards.term: When to use the sine rule
flashcards.definition: When a side and its opposite angle are both known (a complete pair), plus one more side or angle.
a squared = b squared + c squared - 2bc cos A, with A the included angle.
cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / 2bc, where a is the side opposite the wanted angle.

flashcards.term: When to use the cosine rule
flashcards.definition: Two sides and their INCLUDED angle (for the third side), or all three sides (for an angle).
Cos of an obtuse angle is negative, so -2bc cos A becomes a PLUS and the answer grows.
Area = half x a x b x sin C, for two sides a and b and their INCLUDED angle C.
flashcards.example: Sides 7 and 9, included 50 deg: 0.5 x 7 x 9 x sin 50 = 24.1 cm squared.

flashcards.definition: At an included angle of 90 degrees the cosine rule collapses to Pythagoras, because 2bc cos 90 = 0.
Angles total 180 degrees: knowing two angles means the third, which often creates the pair the sine rule needs.
Reduce a 3D problem to two flat right-angled triangles: a diagonal in the base plane, then a vertical section using that diagonal.
flashcards.example: Cuboid base 10 by 7, height 6: base diagonal 12.21, then angle with base = tan^-1(6/12.21) = 26.2 deg.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, sides $a$, $b$ and $c$ are named so that side $a$ is
choices: the side touching angle $A$ on the right
questions.explanation: Each side takes the lowercase letter of the angle it FACES. Side a is opposite angle A and does not touch it — that pairing is what makes the rules work.

questions.stem: In a triangle, $A = 30^\circ$, $a = 6$ cm and $B = 90^\circ$. Use the sine rule to find $b$.
questions.explanation: b = a x sin B / sin A = 6 x sin 90 / sin 30 = 6 x 1 / 0.5 = 12 cm. The option 3 cm comes from multiplying by sin 30 instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides $b = 8$ cm and $c = 10$ cm with included angle $A = 30^\circ$. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area = 0.5 x 8 x 10 x sin 30 = 0.5 x 80 x 0.5 = 20 cm squared. The 40 option forgets the half, 80 forgets both the half and the sine, and 34.6 uses cos instead of sin.

questions.stem: In the cosine rule $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A$, setting $A = 90^\circ$ gives
questions.explanation: Cos 90 = 0, so the entire 2bc term disappears and the cosine rule collapses to Pythagoras. That is why the sine and cosine rules generalise right-angled trig to every triangle.

questions.stem: To use the cosine rule to find side $a$, the information you need is
choices: sides $b$ and $c$ and the included angle $A$
any two sides and any angle
sides $b$ and $c$ and the angle opposite one of them
questions.explanation: The cosine rule for a side needs two sides and the angle BETWEEN them (the included angle). Two angles and a side is instead the territory of the sine rule.

questions.stem: In a triangle, $a = 9$ cm, $A = 40^\circ$ and $b = 7$ cm. Use the sine rule to find angle $B$, to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: sin B = 7 x sin 40 / 9 = 0.500, so B = sin^-1(0.5) = 30.0 deg. Side b is shorter than side a, so angle B must be smaller than angle A = 40 deg: the 150 deg option is impossible.

questions.stem: A triangle has $b = 5$ cm, $c = 8$ cm and included angle $A = 60^\circ$. Find side $a$.
questions.explanation: a^2 = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x cos 60 = 89 - 40 = 49, so a = 7 cm. The option 49 forgets the square root, and 9.43 comes from leaving out the 2bc cos A term.

questions.stem: A triangle has $b = 6$ cm, $c = 10$ cm and included angle $A = 120^\circ$. Find side $a$, correct to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Cos 120 = -0.5, so a^2 = 36 + 100 - 2 x 6 x 10 x (-0.5) = 136 + 60 = 196 and a = 14.0 cm. The option 8.72 cm comes from treating cos 120 as +0.5.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides $a = 7$ cm, $b = 5$ cm and $c = 3$ cm. Find the size of angle $A$.
questions.explanation: cos A = (25 + 9 - 49) / (2 x 5 x 3) = -15/30 = -0.5, giving A = cos^-1(-0.5) = 120 deg. A negative cosine means the angle is obtuse; 60 deg is the sign error.

questions.stem: A triangle has two sides of $7$ cm and $9$ cm, and the angle between them is $50^\circ$. What is its area, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: Area = 0.5 x 7 x 9 x sin 50 = 31.5 x 0.766 = 24.1 cm squared. The option 20.3 uses cos 50 instead of sin 50, 31.5 is the product of the half and the sides without the sine, and 48.3 omits the factor 0.5.

questions.stem: An equilateral triangle has sides of length $8$ cm. What is its area, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: All angles of an equilateral triangle are 60 deg, so area = 0.5 x 8 x 8 x sin 60 = 32 x 0.866 = 27.7 cm squared. The option 32.0 drops the sine, and 55.4 doubles the answer.

questions.stem: In a triangle, $A = 35^\circ$, $B = 65^\circ$ and $a = 10$ cm. Find side $b$, correct to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: b = 10 x sin 65 / sin 35 = 15.8 cm. The option 17.2 is side c (opposite the third angle, 80 deg), and 6.33 flips the sines upside down.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of $6$ cm and $10$ cm, and the angle between them is $120^\circ$. Work out the third side and the area.
questions.explanation: Cos 120 = -0.5, so a^2 = 36 + 100 + 60 = 196 and a = 14.0 cm; area = 0.5 x 6 x 10 x sin 120 = 26.0 cm squared. The 52.0 option omits the factor 0.5, and 8.72 uses +0.5 for cos 120.

questions.stem: A cuboid has a rectangular base $10$ cm by $7$ cm and height $6$ cm. A rope runs in a straight line from a corner of the base to the diagonally opposite top corner. What angle, to 1 decimal place, does the rope make with the base?
questions.explanation: The base diagonal is the square root of 100 + 49 = 12.21 cm (a right-angled triangle in the floor). The rope, that diagonal and the vertical height 6 form a second right-angled triangle: tan of the angle = 6/12.21, giving 26.2 deg. The 31.0 and 40.6 options use a single base edge instead of the diagonal.

questions.stem: In a triangle, two of the angles are $55^\circ$ and $65^\circ$, and the side opposite the $55^\circ$ angle is $9$ cm. What is the length of the LONGEST side, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: The third angle is 180 - 55 - 65 = 60 deg, so the largest angle is 65 deg and the longest side faces it: 9 x sin 65 / sin 55 = 9.96 cm. The option 9.51 cm is the side opposite the 60 deg angle (the middle side), and 8.13 cm comes from swapping the sines.
